newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-W. Australia 97/98 growth rate seen doubling.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-W. Australia 97/98 growth rate seen doubling.

text.p: Economic growth in Western Australia in 1996/97 will be lower than in the last fiscal year but will accelerate in 1997/98 to about 8.75 percent, the Western Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said on Monday.

In its half yearly review of the state economy, the chamber said activity was subdued and sluggish for most of 1996 and by September, Western Australia was no longer the strongest performer of the Australian states.
"This slowing in economic activity should be temporary (however)," it said.
"Growth is forecast to recover strongly to around 8.75 percent in 1997/98, driven by stronger domestic demand and further growth in exports."
It forecast state growth would slow to 4.0 percent in 1996/97 from 6.2 percent in 1995/96.

The chamber said its latest forecasts, produced by the its Economic Research Service, are based on a new model of the state economy which it described as experimental and cautioned that the forecasts should be treated accordingly.
It said real state product growth fell by 1.8 percent between June and September 1996. The fall was broadly based, with consumption, business investment and housing investment all down.
"Net trade made a small positive contribution, but only public investment rose significantly in the quarter," it said.
"Private consumption fell by 2.3 percent and accounted for around two-thirds of the drop in state product."

The new model, however, suggests accelerating economic growth in the coming 18 months. The chamber said consumption growth should be stronger in the December quarter, and the drop in business investment is unlikely to be sustained.
Housing activity and employment growth are also expected to pick up this year.
"In summary, over 1995/96 there was a marked gap between strong aggregate growth figures and the weak performance of many parts of the economy," the chamber said.
"In the second half of 1996 the economic data painted a more consistent picture of economic activity, but it was consistently weak.

"This consistency is likely to persist through 1997, but in a more favourable economic climate. Growth is likely to pick up over 1997 and into 1998 and that stronger growth should be more broadly based than the investment and export surge which contributed most of the strong GSP product recorded to June 1996.

"From early 1997 housing activity is forecast to pick up, followed by consumption and employment from the middle of the year. Business investment and net exports will still be important contributors to economic growth, but they they will not dominate it," the chamber said.
